newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden summons Argentine envoy over 1977 kidnap.
newsitem.headline: Sweden summons Argentine envoy over 1977 kidnap.

text.p: The Argentine ambassador was summoned to Sweden's foreign ministry on Monday to hear of Stockholm's anger at failure by Buenos Aires to cast light on the kidnapping of a teenage Swedish student 20 years ago.
Dagmar Hagelin disappeared on January 27, 1977. Sweden says it suspects she was kidnapped and murdered by troops led by Captain Alfredo Astiz, who is wanted in France for human rights crimes.
"I and the entire Swedish government are still determined to clear up the fate of Dagmar Hagelin," Foreign Minister Lena Hjelm-Wallen said in a statement.

Astiz, dubbed "The Blond Angel" by the media, has become a symbol of impunity for the human rights violations of the 1976 to 1983 military regime. He retired from active service last year without being punished despite having being sentenced to life in jail by a French court.
Astiz is accused of murdering two French nuns, Leonie Duquet and Alice Domon, snatched from a Buenos Aires church in 1977.
Like all officers in Argentina's so-called Dirty War against left-wing guerrillas, Astiz was granted an amnesty by a civilian government in 1987.
"Even if there is no longer the possiblity to prosecute the guilty, the Swedish government will continue to strive to find out exactly what happened to Dagmar Hagelin," Hjelm-Wallen said.

Dagmar's father Ragnar, who has campaigned for 20 years to bring the guilty to trial and find out exactly what happened to his daughter, told Swedish radio he would continue his efforts until he died.
He said it had now been established that Dagmar had been mistakenly identified by the Argentine military.
She knocked on the apartment door of a friend in Buenos Aires. She did not realise that the friend had been arrested the day before and that Argentine soldiers were waiting in the apartment.
Suspecting she was someone else, soldiers tried to arrest her and the young Swede tried to run away.
Eyewitnesses have said she was shot and thrown into the back of a car and taken to an infamous torture centre at the Navy School of Mechanics (ESMA).
Thousands of ESMA detainees were reported to have been drugged, stripped and thrown out of "death flights" over the River Plate and Atlantic Ocean.

In an emotional letter published in the Swedish daily Dagens Nyheter on Sunday, Dagmar's father said it was time for Sweden to drop the quiet diplomacy urged upon him and become more aggressive in its quest for the truth.
